query: For high-entropy alloys used in thermal-insulation applications, what testable hypothesis could be made about an unspecified predictive approach for accurately identifying materials with low phonon thermal conductivity? The hypothesis should explain why the approach would work, predict its improvement over current predictions, define its applicability limits, identify supporting evidence, and specify a decisive experimental benchmark and outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Integrating first‐principles phonon dispersion calculations with statistical modelling of force‐constant fluctuations will more accurately predict low lattice thermal conductivity in high-entropy alloys (HEAs) than current empirical or simplified models.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase, homogeneously mixed high-entropy alloys (e.g., FeCoCrMnNi-type systems) exhibiting severe lattice distortion.
generation.intervention: Apply the predictive approach—which uses DFT-based phonon dispersion calculations combined with statistical distributions of local force-constant fluctuations—to simulate the phonon scattering processes in HEAs.
generation.conditions: Measured at room temperature (and possibly extended to low temperatures) under conditions ensuring a stable, single-phase structure with uniform elemental distribution.
generation.structural_mediator: Lattice distortion and local variations in force constants arising from the random atomic environment in HEAs.
generation.mechanism: Severe lattice distortions in HEAs induce force-constant fluctuations that enhance phonon scattering. By explicitly modelling these fluctuations, the approach can accurately capture the attenuation in the acoustic phonon modes, which govern the low thermal conductivity observed in these materials.
generation.predicted_outcome: The approach will predict phonon dispersion curves and attenuation rates that correlate strongly with reduced lattice thermal conductivity. In practice, the method should identify HEAs with κL values significantly lower than those predicted by conventional empirical mixing rules, showing improved predictive accuracy against benchmark experimental data.
generation.baseline: Current prediction methods based on empirical mixing rules or simplified models that do not fully account for the random force-constant fluctuations in HEAs.
generation.boundary: The predictive model is applicable only to single-phase, well-mixed HEAs. Its accuracy may degrade for multiphase systems or alloys with significant compositional segregation, where the assumptions about homogeneity and force-constant variability do not hold.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative accuracy in capturing the exact magnitude of force-constant fluctuations and temperature-dependent scattering mechanisms remains uncertain. Scaling the approach to more complex or less ideal HEA systems is also less certain.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a series of single-phase HEAs with systematically varied elemental compositions to modulate lattice distortions. Use inelastic neutron or X-ray scattering to experimentally determine the acoustic phonon dispersion and attenuation in these alloys, and measure their lattice thermal conductivity over the desired temperature range.
measurements: Phonon dispersion curves (via inelastic neutron or X-ray scattering)
Lattice thermal conductivity (using appropriate thermal diffusivity methods)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the experimental measurements of phonon attenuation and lattice thermal conductivity do not show a statistically significant improvement in prediction accuracy compared to the baseline empirical models (i.e., if predicted low κL values do not correlate with measured values across the HEA series), then the predictive approach is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Recently, entropy engineering has been used as a novel strategy to optimize the electrical and thermal transport properties of TE materials. By increasing element species, the mixing entropy in a material system increases quickly, and high-entropy materials with over five principal elements will be formed. Severe lattice distortion is usually the core phenomenon of high-entropy material—such distortion leads to strong scattering for heat-carrying phonons and results in low lattice thermal conductivity. Stabilizing single-phase structures by increasing entropy weakens the phase-boundary electron scattering in multiphase high-entropy material, thus providing a beneficial contribution to improve electrical transport properties, i.e., entropy-driven structural stabilization,. Therefore, the high-entropy-stabilized composition should work as a good matrix for further optimization of TE performance by integrating the traditional optimization strategy.

In conclusion, we have reported the first experimental investigation of the acoustic phonon dispersions in a High-Entropy Alloy, complemented by the GVDOS survey, at room and low temperature. FeCoCrMnNi is a 5-element random alloy, and, despite the inherent disorder, its phonon dynamics closely resemble that of the pure elements composing it and the corresponding binary alloys. More specifically, acoustic phonons disperse throughout the whole Brillouin zone up to energies between 20 and 30 meV, exhibiting an attenuation stronger than in simple elements, but of the same order of magnitude as in binary alloys. The whole attenuation behavior can be understood in terms of scattering from force-constant fluctuations, which have been estimated to amount to ~20% using a simple theoretical model, a value comparable with calculations of Mu and co-authors on binary and ternary alloys made of the same elements. cited_evidence.text: Using the same approach, the value of κL was computed for various temperatures in the range 300–700 K (Figure 9). At 300 K, the κL value is 0.4 W K−1 m−1, which is a very low value of the lattice thermal conductivity, favorable for thermoelectric materials. This is due to the lattice distortion effect of high-entropy alloys that can reduce phonon velocity and enhance phonon scattering, resulting in low thermal conductivity. Additionally, one can observe that when the temperature rises, the thermal conductivity of the lattice decreases, which is also due to an increase in phonon scattering at higher temperatures.
